description: How suffering challenges belief in a loving God, and Catholic responses including Augustine and Irenaeus.
content_html:
The Problem of Evil

The problem of evil is one of the oldest challenges to religious belief. If God is omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing) and all-loving, why does suffering exist? A God with all three attributes would have the power to prevent suffering, the knowledge to know about it, and the love to want to stop it. Yet suffering clearly exists — in disease, natural disaster, war and personal tragedy. This logical tension, sometimes called the Epicurean trilemma, leads some thinkers to conclude that either God does not possess all three attributes, or God does not exist.

The Bible does not ignore this question. Isaiah 45 acknowledges God as the one who creates both light and darkness, both peace and disaster. The Psalms also wrestle with it: Psalm 119 contains long passages of praise and lament as the writer turns to God during suffering, trusting in his word even when circumstances suggest abandonment. The book of Job is perhaps the most extended biblical engagement with the problem: Job loses his health, family and property without any obvious cause, and the bulk of the book is his anguished questioning of God and God’s eventual response from the whirlwind. Catholics do not read these texts as providing a neat intellectual solution — instead, they model the posture of honest prayer and trust in God’s ultimate justice.

Key Fact

Philosophers distinguish two kinds of evil: moral evil (suffering caused by human choices — war, murder, abuse) and natural evil (suffering from non-human causes — earthquakes, disease, famine). Moral evil raises questions about God’s purpose in creating free beings; natural evil is harder to explain by appeal to human freedom alone.

Augustine’s Free-Will Defence

St Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE) argued that evil is not a positive thing God created. It is, instead, the privation of good — the absence or corruption of something good, just as darkness is not a substance but the absence of light. God did not create evil; he created a good world. Evil entered through the Fall, when humanity freely chose to disobey God. This applies to both moral evil (direct human wrongdoing) and, in Augustine’s view, natural evil (the disorder that followed the Fall and damaged creation as a whole).

Augustine’s key move is to protect God’s goodness by insisting that the source of evil lies in creaturely freedom, not in God. God gave humans free will — the capacity to choose good — because love chosen freely is infinitely more valuable than love compelled. By choosing evil, humanity brought suffering on themselves and, in Catholic theology, on creation as a whole. Augustine found support for this in the opening chapters of Genesis, where the Fall narrative shows human disobedience introducing pain, conflict and death into a previously harmonious creation.

One of the most common errors in RS exams is attributing the “soul-making” theodicy to Augustine. Augustine’s response is the free-will defence: evil is the privation of good, caused by the misuse of human freedom at the Fall. The soul-making theodicy — that evil is necessary for moral and spiritual development — belongs to St Irenaeus (c.130–202 CE), developed in the modern era by John Hick. If the exam question names “Augustine,” write about privation of good and the Fall. If it names “Irenaeus” or “soul-making,” write about moral development through challenge. Never swap them.

Irenaeus and the Soul-Making Theodicy

St Irenaeus offered a different kind of response. He argued that humans were not created perfect — they were created “in the image” of God (imago Dei) but needed to grow into the “likeness” of God. We are created as children who need to develop through challenge and experience. Suffering and moral struggle are the means by which human beings develop virtues like courage, compassion and patience. A world without challenge or risk would be a world in which no real growth or character formation could take place.

This idea was developed in the twentieth century by philosopher John Hick in Evil and the God of Love (1966). Hick described the world as a “vale of soul-making” — a place designed for moral and spiritual development rather than immediate comfort. On this view, God allows suffering because a pain-free world would produce no virtuous characters, no heroes of sacrifice, no genuine love of God chosen freely through difficulty. Hick also introduced the idea of “epistemic distance” — God remains somewhat hidden so that humans can freely choose to trust him rather than being overwhelmed by his immediate presence.

Key Fact

The soul-making theodicy was proposed by St Irenaeus (c.130–202 CE) and developed by John Hick in Evil and the God of Love (1966). It argues that evil and suffering are necessary for human beings to develop virtues and grow into the likeness of God. A world free of all challenge would be a world in which no real moral character could form.

Catholic Practical Responses: Prayer and Charity

Beyond philosophical theodicy, Catholics respond to suffering through practical action. Prayer is the primary response — turning to God in the midst of suffering, as the Psalms model, trusting that God hears and responds even when the reasons for suffering are not clear. Psalm 119 demonstrates this posture of trust: the writer cries out to God in distress yet returns repeatedly to the theme of delight in God’s word. Charity is the other key response: Catholics are called to address suffering directly through work with the poor, the sick and the marginalised. Organisations like CAFOD embody this in their global relief work.

Augustine’s free-will defence has been challenged on the grounds that natural evil (earthquakes, disease) cannot plausibly be attributed to human misuse of freedom — viruses do not choose to harm. The soul-making theodicy has been challenged because the amount of suffering in the world seems vastly disproportionate to what is needed for moral growth — the Holocaust, childhood cancer, and mass famines cannot be explained as mere educational experiences. Non-religious critics, including Humanists, argue that both theodicies are attempts to rationalise the actions of a God who does not exist. Catholics respond that no theodicy fully dissolves the mystery of suffering — but that the model of Christ on the cross, God entering into suffering rather than standing outside it, offers something more than argument: a personal response to human pain.
exam_tip_html: The most dangerous error on problem-of-evil questions is swapping Augustine and Irenaeus. Fix this now: Augustine = free-will defence + privation of good + the Fall. Irenaeus (developed by Hick) = soul-making + moral development. For the 5-mark source question, cite the Psalm (e.g. “Psalm 119 shows the writer turning to God’s word in suffering”) or Job as your source — these are the named biblical anchors in the spec. For the 12-mark Discuss, develop the Humanist counter-argument in full: they argue that theodicies are unconvincing because the scale of suffering is too great, or because natural evil cannot be explained by free will. Respond from the Catholic position. SPaG marks: spell “theodicy,” “privation,” “omnipotent,” “omniscient” correctly.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The problem of evil challenges belief in God: if God is omnipotent, omniscient and all-loving, why does suffering exist? Catholics distinguish moral evil (from human choice) and natural evil (non-human causes).
  • Augustine (354–430 CE) argues evil is the privation of good caused by the Fall — not something God created. Irenaeus (c.130–202 CE), developed by John Hick in Evil and the God of Love (1966), argues evil is necessary for soul-making and moral development.
  • Catholics also respond practically through prayer (modelled in Psalm 119 and Job) and charity, addressing suffering rather than only theorising about it.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which suffering challenges Catholic belief in God.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: if God is all-powerful he could prevent suffering (1); if God is all-loving he would want to prevent suffering (1); the existence of natural evil (earthquakes, disease) which humans did not cause makes it hard to attribute suffering to human free will alone (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe Augustine's free-will defence of God in the face of evil.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Augustine argues evil is not a thing God created but the privation (absence) of good (1); evil entered the world through the Fall — humanity's free choice to disobey God (1); God gave humans free will because freely chosen love is more valuable than compelled love, but this freedom was misused (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Augustine's free-will defence and the Irenaean soul-making theodicy.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Augustine sees evil as the result of a fall from an original state of perfection — humans were created good but chose evil; Irenaeus sees humans as created immature and needing to develop, so suffering is part of the growth process rather than a consequence of a fall (2); Augustine's theodicy focuses on the origin of evil (the Fall) whereas Irenaeus (developed by Hick) focuses on the purpose of evil (moral development/soul-making) (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic responses to the problem of evil, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per response with development; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Prayer — Psalm 119 models the response of turning to God's word in suffering and trusting in his ultimate goodness even when circumstances suggest abandonment (2); Charity — Catholics address suffering practically, following Jesus's example and teachings such as Matthew 25:31-46 which calls Christians to care for the vulnerable (2); source credit for citing Psalm 119, Job, or another named biblical reference explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'The soul-making theodicy gives a more convincing response to the problem of evil than Augustine's free-will defence.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; argument weighs both theodicies and responds to challenges; justified conclusion. May argue soul-making (Irenaeus/Hick) is stronger because it gives purpose to natural evil, not just moral evil, and addresses why God allows suffering rather than just where it came from. Counter: Augustine's privation argument is philosophically coherent and grounded in the Fall narrative; Hick's model faces the disproportionality problem (Holocaust). Both may be challenged as inadequate. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, at least one source. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: theodicy, privation, Augustine, Irenaeus.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some people argue that theodicies fail to solve the problem of evil, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Natural evil (disease, earthquakes) cannot easily be attributed to human free will — viruses do not choose to harm, making Augustine's free-will defence incomplete (2); the scale of suffering — including events like the Holocaust — seems vastly disproportionate to any developmental need, undermining the soul-making theodicy (2); source credit for Job (the Bible's most direct engagement with disproportionate suffering) or Psalm 119 cited explicitly (1).

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes Augustine's response to the problem of evil?
options: Evil is necessary for humans to develop virtues and grow into the likeness of God
Evil is the absence or privation of good, caused by the misuse of free will at the Fall
Evil exists because God is testing human faith, as shown in the book of Job
Evil will ultimately be overcome in a future age of restoration

knowledge_checks.q: Who developed the soul-making theodicy in the twentieth century, building on Irenaeus?
John Hick described the world as a 'vale of _____' — a place designed for moral and spiritual development.
Augustine argued that evil is not a thing God created but the _____ of good.
Match each thinker to their response to the problem of evil:
right: Evil is the privation of good, caused by the Fall
Humans are created immature; evil aids moral growth
Developed the soul-making theodicy in Evil and the God of Love (1966)

flashcard_questions.q: Who is St Augustine, and what are the dates of his life?
flashcard_questions.a: A North African bishop and theologian, 354-430 CE, who developed the free-will defence.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Augustine mean by 'the privation of good'?
flashcard_questions.a: Evil is the absence or corruption of good — not a substance God created, like darkness being the absence of light.

flashcard_questions.q: What role does 'the Fall' play in Augustine's theodicy?
flashcard_questions.a: It is the moment when humanity freely chose to disobey God, introducing moral and natural disorder into creation.
Evil is necessary for humans to develop virtues and grow into the likeness of God — proposed by Irenaeus.

flashcard_questions.q: When did John Hick publish Evil and the God of Love, and what did it argue?
flashcard_questions.a: 1966 — developed Irenaeus's soul-making: suffering is necessary for moral growth in a 'vale of soul-making'.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two types of evil philosophers distinguish?
flashcard_questions.a: Moral evil (from human choices) and natural evil (from non-human causes such as disease and earthquakes).

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Augustine's theodicy better at explaining moral evil than natural evil?
flashcard_questions.a: Free will explains human wrongdoing, but viruses and earthquakes don't involve human choice.

flashcard_questions.q: Which biblical book most directly engages with the problem of disproportionate suffering?
flashcard_questions.a: Job — he loses health, family and wealth without obvious cause, and questions God directly.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Psalm 119 model as a Catholic practical response to suffering?
flashcard_questions.a: Turning to God's word in suffering and trusting in his goodness even when circumstances suggest abandonment.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main Humanist objection to both theodicies?
flashcard_questions.a: The scale of suffering (e.g. the Holocaust) is disproportionate to any educational purpose — God probably doesn't exist.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Catholic cross respond to the problem of evil beyond philosophical argument?
flashcard_questions.a: It shows God entering into suffering himself through Christ, rather than standing outside it.

glossary_terms.definition: The philosophical challenge to belief in an all-powerful, all-knowing, all-loving God posed by the existence of evil and suffering in the world.
A fifth-century North African bishop (354-430 CE) who argued that evil is the privation of good, caused by the misuse of free will at the Fall.
Augustine's description of evil as the absence or corruption of good — not a substance God created, like darkness being the absence of light.
The original sin of Adam and Eve, which Catholics believe introduced moral and natural disorder into God's good creation.
A second-century bishop (c.130-202 CE) who argued humans were created immature and that evil is necessary for moral and spiritual growth.
A twentieth-century British philosopher of religion (1922-2012) who developed Irenaeus's soul-making theodicy in Evil and the God of Love (1966).
Acts of practical help for others in need, motivated by Christian love — seen as a direct response to suffering in the world.

hero_image_caption: Light breaking through storm clouds — a visual metaphor for the Catholic belief that God meets suffering rather than ignoring it
